The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for individual training examples, they have ultimately fallen short due to their inability to directly optimize a target function - a characteristic necessary for efficiently computing the Shapley value. The current approaches can only efficiently do so in specialized scenarios, such as ridge regression, covering specific use cases such as data cleaning and highlighting problematic training examples. A new set of methods aimed at overcoming these limitations is presented in this paper, each of which offers an innovative way to compute the Shapley value with the ability to optimize a target function. The paper's theoretical foundations provide a framework for applying these methods under certain conditions and showcase their optimal performance in scenarios such as data cleaning and highlighting problematic training examples, even when more advanced algorithms are used. Experimental evaluations conducted on real-world datasets highlight the advantages of the proposed approaches over existing solutions in terms of their accuracy, processing speed, and ability to handle diverse machine learning algorithms.

Conductive spectroscopy experiments were performed in a magnetic field applied perpendicularly to the sample plane to examine the effects of pressure. The self-consistent renormalization of the spin susceptibility with the exchange splitting resulted in these resistivity and Hall effect enhancements.

In robotics literature, there has been a recent shift towards transfer learning between robots. However, the transfer of this strategy to human subjects has been overlooked until now. This study bridges this gap by exploring methods to transfer manipulability information from one person to another, which is essential for teaching robots human-like motion. Although elliptical shapes simplify manipulability information, they are unique to specific tasks and cannot be generalized. In contrast, a more comprehensive representation, known as the manipulability measure, includes all joint actuation variables and their relationships. We compared the effectiveness of various methods to transfer manipulability information from one subject to another using this representation. Additionally, these methods were applied to a popular learning-from-demonstration algorithm to enable the transfer of learned tasks. The results show that even simple approaches can successfully transfer manipulability information and facilitate learning. This study demonstrates that existing methods can transfer manipulability information between humans with positive outcomes, which may encourage more efficient robot-human collaboration.

Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve a stable de-Sitter phase, and ensuring the scalars remain heavy compared to the Hubble scale to facilitate single-field inflation.  Additionally, supergravity predicts several non-renormalizable interactions, rendering it an effective field theory that remains valid up to a specific cutoff energy scale, and thus necessitates a re-examination of the scalar potentials and field dynamics to achieve self-consistency at the quantum level.  This thesis, therefore, constructs locally supersymmetric effective field theories of inflation, incorporating recent reforms to the $\mathcal{N}=1$ supergravity formulation that increase the flexibility in the scalar potential space and accommodate KKLT string backgrounds.

Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, efficiently and accurately enables both end-to-end training and model pruning for CNNs, distinguishing itself from previous work with fine-grained architecture analysis and an in-depth examination of the trade-offs between training precision and efficiency. ClickTrain's key components include a novel pruning technique during the training process, an optimized re-growing method for precise results, and a comprehensive evaluation system to determine the ideal balance between training precision and efficiency. Our framework can be applied to various pruning methods and has successfully been tested on several well-known benchmark models, demonstrating its flexibility. In terms of training precision, ClickTrain achieves an impressive 0.7% reduction in error rate while also significantly reducing the training computational cost by approximately 50%. Our framework ClickTrain is available for public use at https://github.com/alexdai-click/ClickTrain.

Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness in Bayesian settings is unclear. The pessimism principle can also be seen as a consequence of infinite pessimism, where the uncertainty in posterior distribution is fully quantified as negative loss. A novel infinite pessimism method is developed to determine an optimal threshold for pessimism quantification based on posterior distribution characteristics, eliminating the need for a hyperparameter. The infinite pessimism method is implemented in Bayesian contextual bandits and Bayesian learning in the offline setting. The resulting algorithms are context-free and context-dependent, respectively, and both can determine optimal treatment regimes under various assumptions. The infinite pessimism method's advantages are demonstrated in both theoretical and experimental settings.

These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, or applying continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of distances. These clustering methods vary conceptually and cannot easily be compared theoretically. To address this, we compare their performance empirically through a simulation study that evaluates their effectiveness in a practical setting. 

This study uses the widely accepted metric of the Silhouette Width to compare clustering methods, considering factors such as cluster size, data dimensionality, sample size, and the level of data complexity which is influenced by the number of distinct features present. Results from this investigation are provided in detail and discussed fully.

Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. This paper presents a straightforward approach to include these variations and correct beam hardening effects. Employing a polychromatic formula allows us to extend traditional reconstructions to account for multiple energy levels, which in turn facilitates the elimination of bias caused by these variations. Our proposed solution is based on an optimization approach and can be efficiently integrated with conventional reconstructions through iterative convergence. Using low energy levels, such as those present in mammography, as a case study, we provide a more comprehensive understanding of the effectiveness of our approach.

Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world Python code, have begun to take advantage of modern multi-core CPUs with efficient SIMD instructions.  A novel approach to SIMD programming, called vectorized code, uses a strict set of procedures for creating arrays, performing arithmetic operations, and indexing data.  These procedures are specifically designed to optimize performance by minimizing function call overhead on modern CPUs.  By adopting this programming model, Python code can achieve significant speedups of up to 70x when run on modern CPUs with multi-core architectures that include SIMD extensions such as SSE, AVX, and AVX-512.  A new Python module, called `vecpy`, provides a set of high-level tools that enable Python developers to write vectorized code using the traditional Python syntax while still optimizing performance for modern CPU architectures.  A comprehensive study demonstrates that `vecpy` successfully speeds up multiple challenging Python applications, including a mesh generator, an eigenvalue solver, and a video compression algorithm, on modern CPUs.  A key advantage of `vecpy` is its ability to seamlessly integrate with existing Python code, making it an accessible and efficient tool for high-performance computing on modern CPUs.

the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct gaseous structure characterized by its unusually high density. Intertwined with the CMZ are old stars found in numerous globular clusters that form a circular pattern around the center of the galaxy. Studies of gas within the CMZ have been ongoing but detecting gas in smaller scales within the region has been a significant challenge for researchers. Using data from radio frequency 21-cm radio line observations conducted by the Parkes radio telescope, scientists identified small-scale gas structures within the CMZ. Their findings revealed distinct gas features in approximately 40 separate locations that express a specific magnetic field orientation. Data analysis also discovered that these gas structures generally adhere to a specific magnetic field strength of around 100 microgauss. In addition, research revealed that the magnetic field's strength is sufficient to bind small-sized gas loops found within the region. Their magnetic field observations correspond with previous predictions made about the CMZ's magnetic field properties. In essence, their study has successfully measured the magnetic field's effect on individual gas structures within the Central Molecular Zone.

, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Researchers can study valence excitation on the few-femtosecond timescale with this type of XANES spectroscopy, allowing for in-depth examination of electronic dynamics close to the Fermi level.

To develop an enhanced understanding of electronic dynamics under high-fluence conditions, researchers have created a simplified theoretical model, based on recognized physical principles, to elucidate how electronic processes progress. The model effectively translates physical phenomena into mathematical expressions representing key aspects like inverse bremsstrahlung, relativistic photoionization, thermalization, and Auger effects. 

The model allocates a distinct role to each factor and is particularly effective at separating time-dependent effects like nonequilibrium ionization, electron temperature, and long-term self-heat. When compared to experimental results for nickel, the findings reveal impressive consistency between theoretical projections and actual observations. The capabilities of this simplified model will benefit researchers studying electronic processes under even more extreme conditions.

The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies produced by two integrated sine wave generators. The resulting output difference signal, captured by two adjacent pulse width modulation (PWM) circuits, yields a proportional DC output directly linked to the system's temperature. With a simple design that consumes just 10 $\mu$W at 500 kHz sampling rate, this solution offers both rapid temperature sensing and robust immunity to frequency divider multiplications. The proposed solution has been successfully demonstrated in a 65 nm CMOS technology platform, capable of accurately measuring temperatures over a 0 to 100 $^{\circ}$C range with a 0.5 $^{\circ}$C resolution.

In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By applying the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entanglement known as continuous-variable entanglement, it is possible to create the desired hybrid entangled states, which are a combination of both discrete and continuous variables. We present two methods of implementing this technique, the first utilizing single photons and linear beam splitters and the second employing continuous-variable entanglement generators and optical squeezers. By analyzing available technology, it is estimated that this approach will be feasible with current technology, enabling significant advancements in the development of entangled quantum bit strings.

It considers the case where points are introduced one by one in a first-in, first-out order and asks how to maintain a geometric tree structure whose edge lengths stay within a constant multiple of the optimal span for each new point added to the dataset. The research starts by examining the problem in one dimension, where a specific online algorithm achieves nearly linear addendum for adding a point, and then adapts this result to multi-dimensional scenarios, providing addendum bounds for adding a point in d dimensions, such as O(n^(1+1/k)) in k-dimensional space, where k is an integer between 2 and d. Further, the researchers propose an algorithm for maintaining d-dimensional Euclidean spanners with additive k-ambient dimensions stretching factor O(log k * log n / k), providing a k-ambient dimension version of the property for the first time. Lastly, the researchers investigate the problem of determining the minimum addendum needed for maintaining a d-dimensional Euclidean spanner with a given number of points n, and show it is at least the optimal k-ambient dimension for fixed n and k, and then for fixed k and large n, as well as providing an almost-linear lower bound in n for the general addendum problem.

Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, with positive outcomes; yet current approaches disregard the costs involved in extracting device features from network data. This study presents a more practical viewpoint, contending that feature extraction comes with expenses varying across distinct features. Moving beyond existing binary misclassification assessments, this work proposes adopting common risk assessment metrics, such as the False Positive Rate and False Negative Rate, as performance indicators. Experimental findings using real-world data confirm that considering feature extraction costs and non-binary risk assessment yields more precise and informative evaluations of the proposed method's performance.

Here we introduce a concept of quantum imaging that utilizes strong illumination and enhanced detection capabilities. Each of these advancements has the potential to contribute to the development of cutting-edge quantum imaging technologies. A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. Cubic graphs that possess the PH-property have been fully characterized by Alahmadi et al. in 2015, suggesting a general approach for constructing Hamiltonian cycles of K_G. However, counterexamples emerge as soon as the order of G exceeds four, indicating the given method to be insufficient. This paper delves deeper into the PH-property, focusing on graphs of order six to twelve to characterize their Hamiltonian cycles of K_G. New theorems are established to generalize previously identified results by Alahmadi et al. for graphs of order six to twelve. Our approach involves determining all pairings of these graphs that create Hamiltonian cycles of K_G, providing a comprehensive classification for the PH-property in these graphs. In doing so, we identify the graph T_6 as a unique representative that characterizes all graphs of order twelve sharing the PH-property.

models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can significantly affect the resulting image. To overcome this challenge, our research focuses on developing a method to determine optimal prompt modifications that result in the desired image output with minimal trial and error. To accomplish this, we propose a novel approach called Mape: a prompt manipulation explorer. At its core, Mape utilizes a learned, flexible representation of the prompt space to identify a sequence of subtle prompt changes leading to the target image output. During exploration, Mape's neural predictor generates various prompt transformations evaluated against their potential to yield the target image, and it aggregates these possibilities into a flexible, direction-based representation that facilitates text-to-image synthesis. Through this mechanism, Mape shows considerable promise in producing high-quality images and makes meaningful contributions to the field, and it even facilitates generating multiple images from a single prompt with minimal iterations. To support the use of Mape, our project's website provides a publicly accessible diffusion model that allows users to generate image outputs with optimal prompt modifications for free. Alongside this release, our research also includes additional details regarding Mape's development and a range of promising experimental results, as well as a public discussion forum where users can find further information on this project.

a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive cover modeling, which can be implemented using general deep learning workflows. Nevertheless, incorporating disentanglement techniques results in an improved methodology for separating message data from cover data in the model. Consequently, the integration of disentanglement methods proves effective in enhancing the quality of predictive cover models. Inspired by the success of cycleGAN-based methods in reversible steganography, which exploit adversarial networks to learn high-level image features, we introduce a novel method that combines these techniques with disentanglement to analyze the effects on predictive cover modeling. Our approach yields a better-stolen message quality when compared to standard adversarial networks. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the interplay between adversarial and disentanglement losses is provided.

We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When it interacts with the black hole, the droplet loses its mass in the form of Bose-Einstein condensates via tidal forces, causing the black hole to emit gravitational waves. Concurrently, the white dwarf emits electromagnetic waves. Our research reveals that the energy spectrum of these electromagnetic waves has a specific power-law form, with possible observations of this phenomenon being feasible with future telescopes like the James Webb Space Telescope. We also discovered that the efficiency of electromagnetic wave production reaches nearly 10^-3% in certain conditions, which is a much higher rate than similar processes not involving tidal forces.

This novel evaluation method surpasses traditional performance measures by identifying suitable models for each dataset type, and also enables benchmarking outcomes to expand to new, unseen datasets. Ultimately, our work sets the stage for dataset-driven model selection in complex, real-world environments. To understand the influence of this substitution, we investigate transport and magnetic properties, particularly in the series Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10. Bi substitution leads to decreased activation energy and a shift from three-dimensional to one-dimensional behavior in the temperature dependence of the in-plane resistivity. The dimensional cross-over occurs around the same Bi concentration (x ≈ 0.05) that sees the onset of the metal-insulator transition. In the one-dimensional regime, the in-plane resistivity exhibits power-law temperature dependence and mirrors the behavior of the out-of-plane resistivity (which is not the case in the initial stages of the Bi doping). The transition from three-dimensional to one-dimensional behavior is likely a result of the suppression of long-range ferromagnetic order within the series. Moreover, we present direct evidence of a new type of one-dimensional Fermi liquid in the metal-insulator transition regime.

a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple.

on in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex theory. A critical method for resolving this query involves examining the coupling of the Higgs boson with other particles, particularly at high-energy collisions using precision measurements of the Higgs boson's properties. A recent study reported the first-ever measurement of the probability distribution of the Higgs boson decaying into two photons at a 13 TeV energy level, producing the most detailed assessment of this process to date, utilizing a dataset that recorded 36 inverse femtobarns of particle interactions with the ATLAS detector. The measured data points, combined with theoretical predictions of the Higgs boson's behavior, indicate that the likelihood of the Higgs boson accounting for all scalar particles in the Standard Model is less than 1 in  1000 chances, also revealing that the Higgs boson decays into two photons at an rate that differs from the Standard Model's predictions by about 2% in probability.

our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their prediction to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the optimal leakage and the optimal compression rates are attainable by certain deterministic coding strategies, where these goals can be concurrently achieved. We expand upon the initial investigation to consider adversaries that submit multiple guesses and have varying levels of accuracy in matching their predictions to the source sequence. In this extension, we introduce the concept of relative leakage and provide a detailed examination of this parameter for an important class of adversaries known as distinguishable adversaries. The resulting analysis leads to the development of novel single-letter conditions that gauge the adversary's information gain relative to the source code's indistinguishability. These conditions can be interpreted as metric-based requirements for the adversary, where we introduce the term "metric based" to describe the relationship between the adversary's output and the source sequence. Researchers found that in a special type of Hubbard model with strong coupling on a triangular lattice, the dynamical structure factor shows highly localized low-energy excitations near the magnetic ordering wavevector. However, this contrasts with similar models that exhibit magnetic ordering, where a more dispersed low-energy spectrum is typically predicted. Lastly, it was observed that the marginally localized excitations exhibit a specific characteristic behavior when their momentum is near the magnetic ordering wavevector, where their long-term memory, or "hierarchy," shows a strong resemblance to a specific mathematical sequence.

This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is possible that his scientific vision would have been realized through a different methodology if he had mastered mathematics. This criticism of Galileo's scientific method is offered as a counterargument to the widely accepted narrative of his groundbreaking role in shaping science.

a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on their own decisions and judgment.  As a result, these assistants become skilled professionals who work collaboratively with their human colleagues, providing innovative ways to think about complex problems and considering the long-term effects of actions taken.  As these intelligent assistants evolve, they develop their own skills and expertise, contributing to their success and amplifying the capabilities of those with access to them.  This document presents an in-depth analysis of the course's content, providing an introduction, an overview of key topics, and in-depth exploration of the following subjects:  cognitive science, the building of intelligent systems, the creation of collaborative systems, thinking strategies, the development of problem-solving skills, and the intersection of human and machine intelligence.
